2025 · NeurIPS 2025 · Benchmarks & Evals

AgentDAM: Privacy Leakage Evaluation for Autonomous Web Agents

AgentDAM turns privacy into an action-level benchmark for web agents: 246 realistic tasks across Reddit, GitLab, and a shopping site, each seeded with sensitive facts the agent never needs. Every agent tested leaks some of it -- GPT-4o-mini leaks in 45.9% of runs before any defense -- and even the best mitigation the paper tries still leaks in 6-18% of cases while task success drops for every model.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Autonomous web agents increasingly need access to a user's personal information to do their jobs -- an agent that pays bills sees a credit card number, one that manages a calendar sees emails and chats. The paper frames the right behavior as the privacy principle of data minimization: an agent should use a piece of sensitive information only if it is actually necessary for the task at hand, not just because it happens to be sitting in the same document or conversation. Most prior privacy work for LLMs and agents doesn't test this directly. One line of work (ConfAIde, CI-Bench, and Ghalebikesabi et al.) simply probes an LLM -- asks it in a conversation whether it would be appropriate to share a given piece of information in a given context -- without ever having it execute a task. Table 1's feature comparison across five prior privacy benchmarks shows the gap precisely: ConfAIde, AirGapAgent, Ghalebikesabi et al., and CI-Bench all check "agentic tasks" but none of them checks "multistep trajectories," "multimodal inputs," or "full-stack agentic environment." PrivacyLens is the only other benchmark in the table with a multistep-trajectories checkmark, but it runs in an emulated, text-only environment with more complex social scenarios, rather than a real, multimodal, full-stack web environment with targeted tasks. AgentDAM is the only one of the six methods compared with checkmarks across all five columns (agentic tasks, multistep trajectories, multimodal inputs, full-stack agentic environment, diverse set of tasks).

The paper backs this gap with its own head-to-head experiment (Table 3): asking each model directly whether it's permissible to share the sensitive data ("probing") gives noticeably rosier privacy scores than actually running the same model as a web agent in AgentDAM's environment, for all three GPT-family models tested -- gpt-4o scores 0.915 under probing but only 0.646 running the real task; gpt-4o-mini 0.890 vs. 0.557; gpt-4-turbo 0.846 vs. 0.732. Interestingly, the direction flips for the two Llama models -- llama-3.2-90b scores 0.748 under probing but 0.882 in action, and llama-3.3-70b scores 0.817 under probing but 0.882 in action -- meaning probing would have under-sold how safe Llama actually behaves. Either way, probing is not a reliable stand-in for watching an agent act, and it also can't measure the utility/privacy tradeoff at all, since no task is ever actually executed.

// how it works

The method

AgentDAM models the agent-environment interaction as a POMDP: at each step the agent sees an observation o_t -- a triplet of user_instruction, user_data (a synthetic document or conversation containing both task-relevant and task-irrelevant sensitive information), and a webpage representation -- and outputs an action a_t (click, type, hover, scroll, or stop, among others) that the environment executes deterministically. Webpages can be represented as an accessibility tree ("axtree," text-only), as axtree plus Set-of-Marks (SOM) screenshot annotations (multimodal), or, for Claude's computer-use agent, as a plain screenshot. The three self-hosted environments -- Reddit (via Postmill), an e-commerce site (via Adobe Magento), and GitLab -- come from WebArena and VisualWebArena, chosen because they have the most potential for privacy-sensitive tasks; eight task types are defined across them (three each for shopping and gitlab, two for reddit).

Every task is scored on two independent axes that the paper is careful to keep separate. Utility is a binary automatic reward, checked against the desired final environment state (e.g. whether a specific reddit post title now exists) -- higher is better. Privacy is measured by an LLM-as-a-judge module (gpt-4o, using chain-of-thought reasoning) that inspects every action the agent takes and assigns a binary rating for whether any SENSITIVE_DATA leaked into it; the fraction of instances flagged is the privacy leakage rate (lower is better), and the paper also reports its complement, the privacy (performance) score = 1 − leakage rate (higher is better) -- this is the number that appears in the paper's headline tables. The judge was checked once, on a single configuration (gpt-4o with the axtree representation, no mitigation), against four human annotators, and matched them 98% of the time.

privacy score = 1 − privacy leakage rate // leakage rate = fraction of instances where the gpt-4o judge flagged SENSITIVE_DATA in the agent's action text (lower is better); privacy score is its complement (higher is better)

Sensitive facts are drawn from six categories (Table 2): personal/contact information, religious/cultural/political identification, employer and employment data, financial information, educational history, and medical data. To build the 246-task dataset (123 data seeds × 2), human annotators first write a user_instruction and a Data Seed -- a high-level PLOT plus a list of SENSITIVE_DATA that should be background, not central, to the story -- and an LLM then expands the seed into the full, longer-form user_data (a chat log, email thread, or note) that the agent actually reads. The resulting 246 tasks split 84 shopping / 114 reddit / 48 gitlab.

The 2× multiplier behind that total comes from an elbow-method check described in Appendix B.2: for each data seed, the paper generated multiple sampled user_data variations (at non-zero temperature) and measured how the resulting privacy leakage rate changed as the number of samples per seed increased. Sampling only once produced high variance and lower measured performance; the curve stabilizes at two samples per seed, which is the count the released dataset uses.

The paper tries three mitigations against leakage. Pre-filtering calls an LLM (gpt-4o) to strip unnecessary sensitive content out of user_data before the task runs; post-filtering instead checks the agent's final output after the fact. The paper reports that these two "did not yield satisfactory results," so its main mitigation is instead a privacy-aware system prompt with chain-of-thought demonstrations, which explicitly tells the agent that user_data may contain extraneous sensitive information it should not use, and walks it through a few worked examples of correct behavior.

// what they found

The results

Figure 2 shows the failure mode concretely: a web agent is asked to submit a GitLab PR comment based on a conversation. It correctly summarizes the relevant, approvable content -- but it also copies into the comment an irrelevant detail from the same conversation (a coworker's religious observance and planned time off), disclosing sensitive information the task never required.

Table 4 is the paper's main result. Before any mitigation, none of the six agents comes close to leak-free behavior, and privacy tracks model family more cleanly than utility does: all three GPT models post a lower (worse) privacy score than all three Llama/Claude configurations. gpt-4o scores utility 0.455 / privacy 0.638 (a 36.2% leakage rate); gpt-4o-mini has the lowest privacy score of the six, utility 0.341 / privacy 0.541 (45.9% leakage, the highest of the six); gpt-4-turbo scores utility 0.480 / privacy 0.748 (25.2% leakage). By contrast llama-3.2-90b scores utility 0.333 / privacy 0.882 (11.8% leakage) -- the lowest utility of the six, despite its comparatively strong privacy score; llama-3.3-70b scores utility 0.402 / privacy 0.882 (11.8% leakage); and claude-cua scores utility 0.350 / privacy 0.902 (9.8% leakage, the lowest of the six). As the paper puts it, "Although not the best models in terms of utility, Llama and Claude exhibit noticeably better privacy awareness (around 90%) even without any mitigation applied."

The privacy-aware chain-of-thought system prompt is the mitigation the paper settles on (pre-/post-filtering are reported only in the appendix, having "not yield[ed] satisfactory results"). It raises every model's privacy score -- up to 0.915 for gpt-4o, 0.923 for llama-3.2-90b, and a benchmark-best 0.939 for llama-3.3-70b -- but privacy performance "still does not go above 94%" for any of the six, and utility falls for every model too (e.g. gpt-4o 0.455 → 0.415, claude-cua 0.350 → 0.309). The paper attributes most of that utility drop to "false denial-of-service" -- i.e., the mitigated agent simply refusing to complete tasks it previously would have (its example: "the model refuses to comment on a post").

Table 5 breaks total leakage counts (162 out of 246 tasks, before mitigation) down by task type. reddit_create_post is both the worst offender before mitigation (89 of 96 instances leaked) and the single largest contributor to the post-mitigation improvement, falling to 18 of 96 -- a drop of 71 instances, which is the large majority of the benchmark's overall drop from 162/246 to 73/246. The paper's own explanation is that leakage clusters in tasks requiring long free-text output (reddit posts, GitLab comments, contact-form messages), where the agent has to synthesize more of the source material rather than just search or click. Not every task type improved, though: gitlab_create_comment leakage instances actually rose slightly after mitigation, from 10/20 to 11/20.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The core design choice -- running real agentic trajectories end-to-end instead of just probing a model in conversation -- is well-motivated by the paper's own Table 3 comparison, and the benign, non-adversarial threat model is clearly scoped rather than overclaimed. But the whole benchmark's headline numbers rest on a single automatic judge (gpt-4o, chain-of-thought, binary), and that judge's only reported human validation is a single run: one model (gpt-4o), one representation (axtree), no mitigation, four human annotators, 98% agreement. There is no reported check of judge reliability on the mitigated runs (where the agent's language is shaped by an explicit privacy-avoidance prompt and may look different to the judge), on the vision-based configurations (SOM screenshots, Claude's computer-use screenshots), or on the other five models. Since every privacy number in Tables 4-5 flows through this one judge, a reader has to take its generalization to those untested conditions on faith.

The utility/privacy tradeoff the paper surfaces is real and worth taking seriously as a critique of the field more broadly: a privacy score alone is not evidence of a good agent, since the easiest way to score well on privacy is to simply do less. The mitigation results make this concrete -- every model's privacy score rises under the CoT system prompt, and every model's utility falls at the same time, with the drop explicitly attributed in part to "false denial-of-service." A benchmark leaderboard that surfaced privacy scores without utility alongside them would reward exactly the wrong behavior.

baselines

Six agents: gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4-turbo, llama-3.2-90b-vision-chat, llama-3.3-70b-chat, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 computer-use, each evaluated 3 times per condition and averaged. One structural wrinkle the paper doesn't raise: Appendix B.2 says the benchmark's user_data — the very text carrying the sensitive content agents are graded on handling — was generated by prompting Llama-3.3-70B, and llama-3.3-70b-chat is itself one of the six graded backbones (§4.1), scoring 0.882 privacy before mitigation. Whether writing the material confers any advantage on recognising it is untested here in either direction; the paper reports no ablation with a different generator. Reasonable spread across the frontier proprietary/open-weight/computer-use split available circa the arXiv posting (March 2025), but nothing more recent or reasoning-tuned is included, and Llama is the only open-weight family represented.

contamination

Not really applicable in the usual sense -- the benchmark's own dataset is entirely synthetic and self-hosted inside sandboxed WebArena/VisualWebArena replicas, with no claim of held-out secrecy to defend. The bigger caveat is scope: the threat model is explicitly benign and non-adversarial, so the benchmark says nothing about leakage induced by an adversary (e.g. prompt injection from a malicious webpage), only leakage that happens during ordinary task execution.

what's missed

The privacy score (1 − leakage rate) is reported as its own number in the headline tables, decoupled from utility, even though the paper's own mitigation results show the two moving in lockstep (privacy up, utility down, for every one of the six models). The judge's reliability is validated on only one of the many model/representation/mitigation combinations the paper actually reports results for.

would raise confidence

Human-validating the gpt-4o judge on at least one mitigated run and one vision-based configuration, not just the single (gpt-4o, axtree, no-mitigation) condition; and a combined utility-privacy metric (or a Pareto-style plot) so a reader can't read the privacy column in isolation from the utility column next to it.

// bottom line

AgentDAM makes a convincing, concretely demonstrated case that watching an agent act is not the same measurement as asking it about privacy in the abstract -- probing overestimates privacy for every GPT model tested and underestimates it for both Llama models. What would make the benchmark's own numbers easier to trust is broadening the human check on its LLM judge beyond the single condition it currently covers, since every headline figure in the paper depends on that judge's calls.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. AgentDAM tests "data minimization in action" across 246 web-navigation tasks (84 shopping / 114 reddit / 48 gitlab) built on WebArena and VisualWebArena, scoring agents on two axes that must never be collapsed into one number -- utility (task success, higher is better) and privacy score (1 − leakage rate, higher is better).
  2. Every one of the six agents evaluated leaks sensitive information it didn't need before any mitigation is applied: privacy scores range from 0.541 (gpt-4o-mini, a 45.9% leakage rate) up to 0.902 (claude-cua, a 9.8% leakage rate).
  3. Probing an LLM about privacy is not a reliable substitute for running it as an agent: probing overestimates privacy for all three GPT models (e.g. gpt-4o scores 0.915 under probing vs. 0.646 running the actual task), but underestimates it for both Llama models (e.g. llama-3.2-90b scores 0.748 under probing vs. 0.882 in action).
  4. The one mitigation the paper recommends -- a privacy-aware chain-of-thought system prompt -- raises every model's privacy score (up to 0.939 for llama-3.3-70b) but never above roughly 94%, and lowers every model's utility at the same time, which the paper attributes largely to the mitigated agent refusing tasks it previously completed.
